contributions: A dependency-graph representation of a chain of thought, built chunk by chunk into a DAG with each node typed as progress or review, which makes a step's role in the derivation explicit where a linear sequence only records its position.

Two structural redundancy criteria defined on that graph rather than on text or probability: a review node with too few descendants opened a branch that never joined the main line, and a review node past a relative depth threshold is re-verification after the answer.

A three-stage pipeline that installs the behaviour rather than applying the pruner at inference — SFT on pruned traces, DPO over correct trajectories ranked by a redundancy score, then GRPO with a length penalty applied only to correct trajectories and measured against the shortest correct sample per question.
A 42.7% token reduction at 7B with average accuracy rising rather than falling, and a larger effect on the harder benchmarks where overthinking is most expensive.

A length-matched control showing structure-aware pruning holds 93.70% accuracy where truncation to the same length falls to 73.60%, which separates removing the right tokens from removing the right number of tokens.
Behavioural evidence that the trained model changes its own generation habits, with reflection markers falling several-fold and progress connectives rising, rather than merely being cut short.
limitations: The paper has no limitations section. The graph is not derived from the model under study: an external LLM decides every insert-or-merge operation, every node type and every dependency edge, so the pruning inherits that model's judgements, and the validation of those judgements is a human evaluation reported only in an appendix. Chunk boundaries are set by a keyword list, so the units being classified are lexically rather than semantically delimited, which matters because the same keywords are what the method then reports suppressing. Both thresholds are fixed at two descendants and 0.9 relative depth for all experiments with no sensitivity analysis in the main text. The Table 3 control, which is the strongest result, is run on 1000 examples sampled from the training set rather than held out, and its full-CoT accuracy of 98.95% indicates a much easier distribution than the benchmarks in Table 1. The three-stage pipeline also makes attribution hard: the stage-wise ablation shows most of the compression arriving with GRPO and its length penalty, so how much of the 42% is owed to the graph criteria as opposed to a length-penalized RL stage that any pruning scheme could precede is not isolated. Two baselines are adapted reimplementations rather than the authors' originals. Finally, and most consequentially for a reader of this archive: the paper's premise is that redundancy is concentrated in reflection, and its only control is naive length truncation — it never compares against a pruner that ignores reflection, which is the comparison a companion archived study reports as showing no advantage for reflection-targeted methods.
method: The trace is first split into chunks at control tokens such as 'wait' and 'alternatively', then converted into a directed acyclic graph one chunk at a time: an external model (qwen-turbo) is prompted, conditioned on the partially built graph and the current chunk, to either insert a new node or merge the chunk into an existing one, and to assign the node a type and its logical predecessors. Node types are the analytical core — progress nodes advance the reasoning frontier and produce information later steps rely on, review nodes read, check, restate, delete or rewind without advancing it. Two graph properties then define redundancy, both applied only to review nodes. Branch-level redundancy is a descendant count below a threshold, meaning the node opened a narrow side branch that never developed into the main trajectory. Depth-level redundancy is a relative depth above a threshold, meaning the node sits late in the trace and so corresponds to re-verification after the answer was reached. Thresholds are fixed at two descendants and 0.9 relative depth throughout. Surviving nodes are relinearized back into text. That pruned data then drives a three-stage pipeline rather than being used directly: cold-start supervised fine-tuning on the pruned traces, then DPO over pairs of correct trajectories ranked by a redundancy score combining the review-node fraction with normalized length, then GRPO whose length penalty applies only to correct trajectories and is measured as excess over the shortest correct sample for that question. Training uses DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B and 7B, with SFT data from Light-R1, preference data from pre-2024 AIME and pre-2023 AMC, and GRPO on dapo-17k. A separate control compares three trace variants at matched length to ask whether pruning removes essential reasoning.
one_liner: Turns a linear chain of thought into a dependency DAG, labels each node as advancing the frontier or reviewing it, and prunes review nodes on two graph criteria — too few descendants, or too late in the trace — cutting 42% of tokens while accuracy holds or rises.
problem: Reinforcement learning with sparse outcome rewards makes credit assignment over long trajectories hard, and one consequence is overthinking. The paper's specific claim about where that redundancy comes from is inefficient reflection in two forms: indiscriminate reflection, where the model checks every intermediate step including trivial ones, and repetitive reflection, where it re-verifies a conclusion it has already established. Neither adds information to the main chain. Locating them precisely requires knowing which steps depend on which, and a linear trace does not expose that — practical reasoning branches, backtracks and repeats across steps, so a position in the sequence does not say what role a step plays.

relevance.reasoning-training: A twelfth criterion for the archive's redundancy question, and the first that defines redundancy on the derivation structure rather than on a score over tokens or steps. Its length-matched control is the part worth keeping: cutting the same token count by position costs twenty points of accuracy where cutting by graph role costs five, which is direct evidence that redundancy has structure and is not simply tail. That result also gives the archive's efficiency literature a control it has generally lacked, since most sources compare against uncompressed generation rather than against an equal-length naive cut. The paper is also a clean instance of the tension this archive is now tracking. Its whole premise is that redundancy is concentrated in reflection, and the companion study added alongside it reports that pruning methods deliberately targeting reflective statements perform no better than those ignoring them. The two are not strictly contradictory — they use different controls, different settings and different granularity — but this paper cannot resolve the disagreement, because reflection-agnostic pruning is exactly the baseline it never runs.
relevance.test-time-scaling: Attacks the length knob from the training side and reports the outcome this topic usually cannot get: shorter and more accurate at once, 42.7% fewer tokens with average accuracy up. What makes it credible rather than a threshold artefact is that the behaviour is installed rather than imposed — the trained model's own reflection-marker frequency falls several-fold and its length distribution loses the long tail, so the saving appears at inference without an inference-time controller. That is the regime a companion archived study warns about from the other direction, finding that long-CoT students often keep verbose habits despite concise supervision; here the habits do change, which makes the pair worth reading together. The caution is that the compression arrives largely with the GRPO length penalty rather than with the graph criteria, so what generalizes may be the penalty design more than the pruning rule.

results: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B average accuracy rises from 59.72 to 60.95 while average length falls from 8134 to 4660 tokens, a 42.7% reduction, with the largest gains on the harder sets — AIME25 from 29.00 to 31.67 at 12779 to 6977 tokens, and OlympiadBench from 56.77 to 59.85. At 1.5B the average goes from 46.68 to 49.91 with a 36% length reduction, with AMC23 rising 63.12 to 69.38 and MATH500 72.65 to 80.40. The graph statistics show what is being removed: average nodes per trace fall from 27.8 to 15.6 while average review nodes fall from 16.8 to 4.5, so the pruning is concentrated on review nodes as designed, at a total data-synthesis cost of $20. The control experiment is the most informative result. Comparing full traces, graph-pruned traces and length-matched truncation on 1000 examples with eight generations each, full CoT reaches 98.95% accuracy and 99.60% consistency, graph pruning holds 93.70% and 90.69%, while truncating to the same length collapses to 73.60% and 69.10%. Cutting the same number of tokens by position rather than by structure therefore costs twenty points, which is the paper's evidence that what it removes is not merely length. Behaviourally, after training the frequency of reflection markers falls sharply on AIME24 — 'wait' from roughly 92 to 24 occurrences per response and 'but' from 47 to 19 — while the progress connective 'therefore' rises from 13 to 56, and the response-length distribution loses its long tail.
